newsitem.title: USA: U.S. offers aid for Israeli missile defense.
newsitem.headline: U.S. offers aid for Israeli missile defense.

text.p: The United States on Thursday offered to sharply increase financial aid to Israel's anti-missile defence programme, including extra funds for the Arrow missile and a new laser weapon.
The announcement by U.S. Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon followed a meeting between visiting Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai and Defence Secretary William Cohen.

Bacon said American aid for the Arrow programme, which stands at $200 million over five years, could be increased by 25 percent after consultation with Congress. Israel has successfully used the Arrow missile to shoot down test missiles.
"The details aren't totally worked out, but we will increase our investment in the Arrow missile programme and (the investment) will help with testing and other aspects of it," said Bacon.
He gave no additional financial figures, but said the United States had also offered to provide more money for joint work on the U.S. "Nautilus" high-energy laser.
Israel is currently developing the Arrow to shoot down Scud and other missiles. Bacon said Israel considered the weapon very important to its defence.
Israel hopes to use the Nautilus laser to burn up and destroy attacking Katyusha rockets which were fired in large numbers into northern Israel from southern Lebanon last year.
In a statement released after the Cohen-Mordechai meeting, the Pentagon said the two agreed to accelerate the anti-missile programme because it was important to Israeli defence.
Bacon said the United States also agreed to help Israel improve its battle against terrorism but was not specific on that point.

Cohen stressed in a brief exchange with reporters before the meeting that the United States continued to be committed to maintaining Israel's military superiority over other countries in the Middle East region.
The Pentagon notified Congress on Wednesday that Israel planned to buy 15 U.S. UH-60L Blackhawk military helicopters and 34 helicopter engines for an estimated $200 million.

Defence officials said on Thursday that sale of the troop-carrying helicopters, made by United Technology Corp's Sikorsky Aircraft division, and the General Electric Co. engines was another example of Washington's commitment to Israel's defence.
They said that the helicopters would be paid for with some of the more than $3 billion in annual U.S. aid to Israel.
